task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to derive a suppression-conditional recommended mix from historical data without lookahead or outcome leakage?
Can defensive coverages be reliably classified from play-by-play and defensive matchup data?
What adherence metric (e.g., Euclidean distance, KL divergence) best captures strategic fidelity?
How to aggregate game-level adherence to series-level while preserving signal?
How to control for team quality, opponent strength, and series-level confounders with only 54 series?
evidence_establishes: No prior systematic evidence is available for this specific question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing is known about the empirical relationship between adherence to a recommended mix and winning.
No baseline effect size or measurement reliability estimates exist.
own_inferences: The question as posed is extremely ambitious given the small unit count (54 series) and the lack of validated defensive-coverage labels.
A series-level analysis will be underpowered to detect plausible effect sizes, especially after adjusting for multiple confounders.
Even at the game level, inferring coverages from play-by-play and matchup data is noisy, reducing signal-to-noise.

The term 'suppression-conditional' likely implies a model-based optimal mix (e.g., minimizing opponent expected points given a risk constraint); constructing that model without lookahead is possible but adds model uncertainty.
If the recommended mix is defined using the same data that determines winning, the result would be a statistical artifact; a strict temporal split is essential.
uncertainties: No validated coverage-classification algorithm exists in this project; accuracy and recall are unknown.
The precise meaning of 'suppression-conditional' (what parameter defines the condition?) is ambiguous.
The natural unit of a playoff series further limits sample size, but changing to games would violate the recorded unit and raise autocorrelation issues.
It is unclear whether a competent test could distinguish adherence from overall team defensive quality.

historical_effect.explanation: No [prior work] were returned; the assessment relies entirely on methodological and measurement considerations.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 54 playoff series are available as recorded; detecting a moderate effect with adequate power while controlling for team strength and opponent factors is infeasible without a substantially larger unit count (e.g., >200 series).

Defensive coverages must be inferred from play-by-play and matchup data; no validated classification scheme exists, introducing unknown but likely large measurement error that attenuates any true relationship.
Teams with higher adherence may be systematically better defensive teams; separating causal effect from general talent is difficult, especially with small N.

prior_work.summary: No prior project studies on this exact question were retrieved; whether any external work exists is not recorded.

risks.text: With only 54 series, even a large effect size would require many covariates, leading to overfitting or insufficient power.
Coverage assignment (e.g., drop, switch, trap) from noisy play-by-play and matchup data will misclassify possessions; adherence metrics will contain substantial noise.
Team strength, injuries, home-court advantage, and series-specific strategy adjustments all correlate with winning and possibly with adherence.
If the recommended mix is constructed using the same series’ outcomes or game results, adherence would be an artifact of circular reasoning.

The recommended mix derived from historical performances may be biased toward coverages that worked in past small samples, and teams that happened to follow those coverages would appear successful by chance.
If winning outcomes are used to label which coverages suppress scoring best, the recommended mix becomes a function of the very outcome being predicted, invalidating the test.
Adherence measured via opponent points per possession introduces a mechanical link to scoring margin and thereby to winning, conflating strategic adherence with simple defensive effectiveness.
Multiple possible adherence metrics, coverage taxonomies, and suppression conditions create a large researcher degree-of-freedom problem if not pre-registered.
Defensive strategies and officiating emphasis change across seasons; a model of recommended mix trained on 2022-23 may not generalize to 2025-26.

design.estimand: Effect of series-average adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended defensive mix on the probability of winning a playoff series.
design.sample: All 54 completed playoff series from 2022-23 through 2025-26 (partial 2025-26 series excluded if incomplete).
design.power: Negligible for realistic effect sizes; a power analysis assuming a medium Cohen’s d of 0.5 would require >200 series even with few covariates; 54 series yield power <20% for that effect.
design.controls: Pre-series team Elo rating, regular-season net defensive rating, series-average injury-impact minutes, binary home-court advantage, opponent pre-series offensive rating. Random effects for season.
design.falsification: Temporal split: recommended mix built solely from 2022-23 and 2023-24; adherence measured in 2024-25 and 2025-26 series. A placebo test recomputes the recommended mix using scrambled team labels; association should vanish.
design.multiplicity: Primary analysis uses a single, pre-registered coverage taxonomy (e.g., five-category: drop, switch, trap, zone, man-to-man), a single adherence metric (Bhattacharyya distance), and a single logistic regression specification. No subgroup analyses without explicit adjustment.
design.decision_rule: Two-sided Wald test p < 0.05 on the adherence coefficient in a logistic regression predicting series win, with a pre-registered minimum sample size of 150 series before interpreting results (thus the test is pre-emptively inconclusive with current data).
design.data_version: NBA stats API, play-by-play, rotation, matchups, summary, and derived play-type possessions, as frozen for the 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons.
